extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians interested in foundations, and graduate students studying concepts/definitions in mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological guidance for judging, choosing, and revising mathematical concepts and definitions (e.g., when a school definition should be replaced by a more explanatory algebraic one). Emphasizes naturalness, fruitfulness, explanatory role, and the Riemann–Dedekind synthetic style of choosing basic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Port Royal principle (classify and define well)
rubrics_metrics.description: “nothing is more important in science than classifying and defining well ... [though] it depends much more on our knowledge of the subject matter being discussed than on the rules of logic.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat classification and definition as central methodological tasks; anchor choices in detailed knowledge of the subject matter rather than in purely formal logical rules. Use historical and mathematical practice as benchmarks for what counts as good classification/definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness vs. artificiality of concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish natural properties from artificial (grue-like) ones; natural properties are those that warrant being counted as the ‘proper’ or important features for classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naturalness is not read off syntax of a definition; it is embedded in mathematical method and must be assessed by looking at mathematical practice, explanatory connections, and role in important arguments (e.g., the Legendre symbol counted as natural despite a disjunctive introductory definition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Projectibility / support for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural properties are linked to projectibility: Natural properties (‘green’) support correct predictions and artificial ones (‘grue’) don’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inductive success as evidence for projectibility. Mathematical induction-like reasoning (e.g., Euler’s enumerative induction to conjecture quadratic reciprocity) shows that projectibility in mathematics does not depend on physical causation; look for patterns that reliably guide correct conjectures and predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power / fit into explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: A concept is improved if it 'is made to fit better into explanations (or into arguments that are good in some other way)'. Real definitions should serve explanatory roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions that play a central role in explanatory frameworks and in the structure of proofs (for instance, the algebraic definition of 'prime' that underlies major number-theoretic results). Assess definitions by how they help explain a mass of facts and by their contribution to unification and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitfulness / theoretical fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical virtue of a concept measured by its fruitfulness for subsequent research and problem-solving (Kuhn/Nolan-style 'fertility').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge candidate definitions/categories by their historical or plausible future track record: do they generate productive research programs, new results, connections, or simplifications? Use case studies (Riemann/Dedekind examples) to assess fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real definition / identification of essential properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding a 'real definition' amounts to singling out the essential property that explains or grounds a class (e.g., algebraic criterion for primes rather than the elementary school divisibility criterion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'real definitions' as those that function as keys that explain a body of facts, improve concepts, and (possibly) identify essences or causes. Robinson’s useful components include 'searching for a key that will explain a mass of facts' and 'improvement of concepts'. Use explanatory and argumentative roles to identify the 'real' definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement of concepts as an evaluative standard
rubrics_metrics.description: One criterion for improvement: a concept is improved if it better fits into explanations and argument structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify improvement in terms of explanatory integration, unifying power, and enhanced mathematical practice. Avoid treating mere convenience as sufficient; improvement should be tied to deeper explanatory payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective correctness of classification/definition
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be an objectively correct choice of definition or basic categories—i.e., we can really learn something about the subject when we adopt a better definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek tangible sufficient conditions for 'objective correctness' grounded in practice: explanatory success, fruitfulness, and sustained centrality to important arguments. Be explicit about the standards used rather than relying on unanalyzed intuitions about objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of basic categories driven by evidence and fruitfulness (Riemann–Dedekind approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about what to regard as fundamental properties should be part of the scientific/mathematical problem to be solved and judged by later evidence (not antecedently evident).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the methodological stance exemplified by Riemann and Dedekind: choose basic categories that yield fruitful, explanatory formulations, even if they differ from traditional primitives (+, ×). Prefer synthetic treatments that emphasize characteristic properties and conceptual clarity over heavy computation when these yield greater explanatory reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing naturalness to mere pragmatic convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not dismiss the mathematical naturalness of a property as merely pragmatic or mere mathematical convenience without examining the depth of the mathematical rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require substantive mathematical rationale (richness and depth) for claims of naturalness; resist the quick move that all distinctions of natural vs. non-natural are merely pragmatic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dependence/causal-conceptual relations to support definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to conceptual or metaphysical dependence (in lieu of physical causation) to explain how some mathematical facts depend on others and thereby ground explanatory priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ accounts of dependence (e.g., Kim-style dependence) to explicate why certain definitions/ideas 'cause' or ground others in the explanatory structure of mathematics. This supplies a basis for calling some definitions 'real' or essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize partial grasp / implicit conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers may have true thoughts or partial grasp of concepts before a precise definition is formulated; definitions can make explicit previously implicit conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or proposing a definition, consider historical evidence of implicit conceptions (e.g., Newton/Leibniz vs. ε−δ calculus) and whether the new definition captures and clarifies earlier partial grasps rather than inventing unrelated meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address indeterminacy by privileging natural interpretations (Lewis-style roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish intended/natural interpretations among many formally compatible but 'wacky' alternatives by appealing to a class of privileged (natural) properties that underwrite simplicity, similarity, lawlikeness, and correct inductive expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the work that recognition of natural properties does (e.g., underwriting natural/artiﬁcial distinctions, evaluations of simplicity and similarity, singling out intended interpretations) as a criterion when resolving semantic or interpretive indeterminacies in mathematical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and case-based analysis as part of evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical/historical study of how concepts have been adopted and functioned in practice is essential to assessing their value and naturalness (e.g., study of quadratic reciprocity, Legendre symbol, primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground judgments in detailed case studies from mathematics: trace how concepts were used, how they facilitated explanations and research, and how they integrated into central arguments. Philosophical analysis should go hand in hand with such historical/mathematical case work.
